claim: Eighty-eight participants (51 females, mean age = 27 ± 8 years) took part in experiment 1.
source: Eighty-eight participants (51 females, mean age = 27 ± 8 years) took part in experiment 1.
evidence: Direct statement of participant demographics in the manuscript.

claim: Twenty participants had a primary diagnosis of major depressive disorder (MDD).
source: Twenty participants had a primary diagnosis of major depressive disorder (MDD)
evidence: Direct statement of participant diagnostic composition.

claim: Twelve participants had a primary diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder (GAD).
source: 12 participants had a primary diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder (GAD)
evidence: Direct statement of participant diagnostic composition.

claim: Twenty-six 'healthy control' participants of approximately the same age and sex ratio were screened to ensure they were free of any psychiatric diagnosis.
source: 26 'healthy control' participants of approximately the same age and sex ratio were screened to ensure they were free of any psychiatric diagnosis
evidence: Direct statement of control group characteristics.

claim: Thirty participants were members of the local community with a natural range of internalizing symptoms.
source: 30 participants were members of the local community with a natural range of internalizing symptoms
evidence: Direct statement of community sample characteristics.

claim: Data from two control participants was excluded; one was a result of equipment failure; debriefing indicated the second misunderstood the task.
source: Data from two control participants was excluded; one was a result of equipment failure; debriefing indicated the second misunderstood the task.
evidence: Direct statement of data exclusion criteria and reasons.

claim: This left 86 participants in total.
source: This left 86 participants in total.
evidence: Direct statement of final sample size after exclusions.

claim: Bifactor modeling of item level responses provides a simple approach to separate symptom variance common to both anxiety and depression from that specific to depression or to anxiety.
source: Bifactor modeling of item level responses provides a simple approach to achieve this aim, as demonstrated previously within the internalizing literature (Clark et al., 1994; Steer et al., 1995; Steer et al., 1999; Simms et al., 2008; Brodbeck et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature demonstrating this approach.

claim: Bifactor models have consistently revealed a substantial amount of shared variance in internalizing symptoms, often termed 'general distress' or 'negative affect'.
source: It has been used extensively to study the structure of internalizing symptomology (Clark et al., 1994; Steer et al., 1995; Zinbarg and Barlow, 1996; Steer et al., 1999; Simms et al., 2008; Steer et al., 2008; Brodbeck et al., 2011) and has consistently revealed a substantial amount of shared variance, often termed 'general distress' or 'negative affect' (Clark and Watson, 1991; Clark et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Separate specific factors for depression and anxiety are consistently observed in bifactor models, with the depression-specific factor tapping symptoms of anhedonia.
source: In addition, separate specific factors for depression and anxiety are consistently observed, with the depression-specific factor tapping symptoms of anhedonia (Clark et al., 1994; Steer et al., 1999; Steer et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Anxiety-specific factors in bifactor models tap symptoms of anxious arousal and worry.
source: anxiety-specific factors tapping symptoms of anxious arousal (Clark et al., 1994; Steer et al., 1999; Steer et al., 2008) and worry (Brodbeck et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Only the first three eigenvalues were reliably distinguishable from noise in the eigenvalue decomposition of the covariance matrix.
source: Only the first three eigenvalues were reliably distinguishable from noise—this was determined by comparison of the eigenvalues in descending order against eigenvalues obtained from a random normal matrix of equivalent size (Humphreys and Montanelli, 1975; Floyd and Widaman, 1995), see Figure 1—figure supplement 1
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and reference to figure showing eigenvalue decomposition results.

claim: The general factor had high loadings (>0.4) for multiple anxiety-related and depression-related items and moderately high loadings (>0.2) across almost all items.
source: In line with previous findings (Clark et al., 1994; Steer et al., 1995; Zinbarg and Barlow, 1996; Steer et al., 1999; Simms et al., 2008; Steer et al., 2008; Brodbeck et al., 2011), the general factor had high loadings (>0.4) for multiple anxiety-related and depression-related items and moderately high loadings (>0.2) across almost all items.
evidence: Supported by data from bifactor analysis and citations to prior literature showing similar patterns.

claim: One specific factor had high loadings (>0.4) for questions related to anhedonia and depressed mood.
source: One specific factor had high loadings (>0.4) for questions related to anhedonia and depressed mood.
evidence: Direct statement of bifactor analysis results.

claim: The other specific factor had high loadings (>0.4) for questions related to worry and anxiety.
source: The other specific factor had high loadings (>0.4) for questions related to worry and anxiety.
evidence: Direct statement of bifactor analysis results.

claim: The confirmatory bifactor analysis in an independent online sample (n = 199) showed a good fit to the data, with comparative fit index (CFI) = 0.962.
source: This constrained model showed a good fit to the data from this new participant sample, comparative fit index (CFI) = 0.962.
evidence: Direct statement of model fit statistics from confirmatory factor analysis.

claim: The factor loadings obtained from the exploratory bifactor analysis in the second participant sample were highly congruent with the factor loadings obtained from experiment 1, with cosine-similarity of 0.96 for the general factor loadings, 0.81 for the depression-specific factor loadings, and 0.77 for the anxiety-specific factor loadings.
source: The factor loadings obtained were highly congruent with the factor loadings obtained from the bifactor analysis in experiment 1 (cosine-similarity was 0.96 for the general factor loadings, 0.81 for the depression-specific factor loadings, and 0.77 for the anxiety-specific factor loadings).
evidence: Direct statement of quantitative similarity metrics between factor analyses.

claim: Participants' scores on the general factor correlated strongly (r > 0.60) with summary scores for all the questionnaire measures.
source: As can be seen in Figure 1c, participants' scores on the general factor correlated strongly (r > 0.60) with summary scores for all the questionnaire measures, indicating that the general factor is indeed tapping variance linked to both anxiety and depressive symptoms.
evidence: Supported by correlation data presented in Figure 1c.

claim: Scores on the depression-specific factor correlated strongly with scores for the MASQ anhedonia subscale (MASQ-AD; r = 0.72) and the STAI depression subscale (STAIdep; r = 0.53).
source: Scores on the depression-specific factor correlated strongly with scores for the MASQ anhedonia subscale (MASQ-AD; r = 0.72) and the STAI depression subscale (STAIdep; r = 0.53)
evidence: Direct statement of correlation coefficients from data analysis.

claim: Scores on the anxiety-specific factor correlated strongly with scores for the Penn State Worry Questionnaire (PSWQ; r = 0.76).
source: scores on the anxiety-specific factor correlated strongly with scores for the Penn State Worry Questionnaire (PSWQ; r = 0.76).
evidence: Direct statement of correlation coefficient from data analysis.

claim: The additive model (#2) fit participants' choice behavior better than the multiplicative model (#1).
source: We observed that the additive model fit participants' choice behavior better (model #2 PSIS-LOO = 26,164 versus model #1 PSIS-LOO = 27,801; difference in PSIS-LOO = −1637; std. error of difference = 241; lower PSIS-LOO is better).
evidence: Supported by model comparison statistics using PSIS-LOO.

claim: The additive model finding is consistent with observations of separate striatal representations for outcome magnitude and probability.
source: This finding is consistent with observations of separate striatal representations for outcome magnitude and probability (Berns and Bell, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior neuroimaging work.

claim: Additive models have been reported to fit choice behavior better than expected value models in work with non-human primates.
source: as well as findings from work with non-human primates where additive models have also been reported to fit choice behavior better than expected value models (Donahue and Lee, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior animal research.

claim: Including effects of relative outcome value for all three model parameters, including the two-way interactions with block type and task version, improved PSIS-LOO (model #5 PSIS-LOO = 25,462 versus model #2 PSIS-LOO = 26,164; difference in PSIS-LOO = −702; std. error of difference = 142).
source: Including effects of relative outcome value for all three model parameters, including the two-way interactions with block type and task version, improved PSIS-LOO (model #5 PSIS-LOO = 25,462 versus model #2 PSIS-LOO = 26,164; difference in PSIS-LOO = −702; std. error of difference = 142; lower PSIS-LOO is better).
evidence: Direct statement of model comparison statistics.

claim: Allowing subjective weighting of magnitude differences improved model fit (model #7 PSIS-LOO = 25,154 versus model #5 PSIS-LOO = 25,462; difference in PSIS-LOO = −308; std. error of difference = 104).
source: Additional stages of model comparison revealed that allowing subjective weighting of magnitude differences improved model fit (model #7 PSIS-LOO = 25,154 versus model #5 PSIS-LOO = 25,462; difference in PSIS-LOO = −308; std. error of difference = 104)
evidence: Direct statement of model comparison statistics.

claim: The addition of a choice kernel that captures participants' predisposition to repeating prior choices improved model fit (model #11 PSIS-LOO = 25,037 versus model #7 PSIS-LOO = 25,154; difference in PSIS-LOO = −117; std. error of difference = 42).
source: as did the addition of a choice kernel that captures participants' predisposition to repeating prior choices (model #11 PSIS-LOO = 25,037 versus model #7 PSIS-LOO = 25,154; difference in PSIS-LOO = −117; std. error of difference = 42).
evidence: Direct statement of model comparison statistics.

claim: The recovered parameters from simulated datasets strongly correlated with the ground truth parameter values; the mean correlation across simulated datasets and across parameters was r = 0.76 (std = 0.15).
source: The recovered parameters from each dataset strongly correlated with the ground truth parameter values; the mean correlation across simulated datasets and across parameters was r = 0.76 (std = 0.15).
evidence: Direct statement of parameter recovery analysis results.

claim: For learning rate components, the average correlation in parameter recovery was r = 0.88 (std = 0.13).
source: For learning rate components, the average correlation was r = 0.88 (std = 0.13)
evidence: Direct statement of parameter recovery analysis results for learning rate.

claim: Participants had higher learning rates during the volatile block than the stable block.
source: Participants had higher learning rates during the volatile block than the stable block
evidence: Supported by posterior distributions showing credible effect of block type on learning rate.

claim: Participants had higher learning rates during the aversive task than the reward gain task.
source: higher learning rates during the aversive task than the reward gain task
evidence: Supported by posterior distributions showing credible effect of task version on learning rate.

claim: Participants had higher learning rates on trials following good versus bad outcomes.
source: higher learning rates on trials following good versus bad outcomes
evidence: Supported by posterior distributions showing credible effect of relative outcome value on learning rate.

claim: Individuals with low scores on the general factor adjusted learning rate between the stable and volatile task blocks to a greater extent than individuals with high general factor scores.
source: Individuals with low scores on the general factor adjusted learning rate between the stable and volatile task blocks to a greater extent than individuals with high general factor scores.
evidence: Interpretation of the negative regression coefficient for general factor on learning rate adjustment.

claim: The ability to appropriately adjust learning rate to volatility, previously linked to trait anxiety, is actually common to both anxiety and depression and not specific to one or the other.
source: This suggests that the ability to appropriately adjust learning rate to volatility, previously linked to trait anxiety (Browning et al., 2015), is actually common to both anxiety and depression and not specific to one or the other.
evidence: Inference drawn from the finding that general factor but not specific factors modulate learning rate adjustment, combined with citation to prior work.

claim: Low general factor scores were associated with higher learning rates following good versus bad outcomes, both when outcomes were reward-related and when they were aversive.
source: Low general factor scores (shown in blue) were associated with higher learning rates following good versus bad outcomes, both when outcomes were reward-related (here a good outcome was a reward) and when they were aversive (here a good outcome was no shock delivery).
evidence: Interpretation of modeling results illustrated in Figure 4b.

claim: Low general factor scores were associated with a more pronounced difference in learning rate between volatile and stable task blocks following good outcomes, observed both when outcomes were reward-related and aversive.
source: Low general factor scores were also associated with a more pronounced difference in learning rate between volatile and stable task blocks following good outcomes. This was observed both when outcomes were reward-related and aversive.
evidence: Interpretation of modeling results illustrated in Figure 4b.

claim: The boost in learning from positive predictions errors under volatile conditions shown by individuals with low general factor scores was absent in individuals with high general factor scores.
source: In particular, the boost in learning from positive predictions errors under volatile conditions (i.e. from good relative outcomes in the volatile block) shown by individuals with low general factor scores was absent in individuals with high general factor scores
evidence: Interpretation of modeling results illustrated in Figure 4b.

claim: Individuals with high general factor scores' learning after positive outcomes was reduced under volatile relative to stable conditions.
source: if anything individuals with high general factor scores' learning after positive outcomes was reduced under volatile relative to stable conditions.
evidence: Interpretation of modeling results illustrated in Figure 4b.

claim: Parameter recovery analysis revealed successful recovery of the parameter representing the three-way interaction of block type, relative outcome value and task type on learning rate.
source: We note that a parameter recovery analysis revealed successful recovery of the parameter representing the three-way interaction of block type, relative outcome value and task type on learning rate (Appendix 4—figure 5).
evidence: Reference to parameter recovery analysis results shown in appendix figure.

claim: The negative relationship between general factor scores and increased learning rate following relative good outcomes in volatile environments did not differ credibly as function of task version (reward, aversive).
source: Together, these findings support the conclusion that the negative relationship between general factor scores and increased learning rate following relative good outcomes in volatile environments did not differ credibly as function of task version (reward, aversive).
evidence: Inference drawn from the non-credible three-way interaction and successful parameter recovery.

claim: One-hundred and seventy-two participants were recruited from Amazon's Mechanical Turk platform to participate in Experiment 2.
source: One-hundred and seventy-two participants were recruited from Amazon's Mechanical Turk platform to participate in Experiment 2
evidence: Direct statement of participant recruitment for experiment 2.

claim: Twenty-five participants were excluded from experiment 2 for having greater than 10 missed responses in each task, leaving 147 participants for analysis.
source: We excluded participants who missed 10 or more responses in either the reward gain or reward loss version of the volatility task (the task is detailed further below); this left 147 participants (n = 147; 65 females) whose data were included in the analyses.
evidence: Direct statement of exclusion criteria and final sample size.

claim: Participants in experiment 2 showed similar distributions of scores on the STAI, MASQ, and BDI to participants in Experiment 1.
source: Participants filled out the Spielberger State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI), the Mood and Anxiety Symptoms Questionnaire (MASQ), and the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), showing similar distributions of scores across these three measures to participants in Experiment 1
evidence: Direct statement comparing questionnaire score distributions across experiments.

claim: Factor scores calculated using the full versus reduced item set showed little change for the general factor (r = 0.97) or the depression-specific factor (r = 0.97).
source: This revealed little change in scores for the general factor (r = 0.97) or the depression-specific factor (r = 0.97).
evidence: Direct statement of correlation analysis results comparing factor scores.

claim: Scores on the anxiety-specific factor were only moderately correlated when using loadings from the full versus reduced set of items (r = 0.41).
source: Scores on the anxiety-specific factor were only moderately correlated when using loadings from the full versus reduced set of items (r = 0.41)
evidence: Direct statement of correlation analysis results.

claim: The moderate correlation for the anxiety-specific factor likely reflects the omission of the PSWQ from the reduced questionnaire set.
source: this likely reflects the omission of the PSWQ from the reduced questionnaire set.
evidence: Inference about the cause of reduced correlation based on questionnaire content.

claim: In experiment 2, individuals with low general factor scores showed greater adjustment of learning rate to volatility than participants with high general factor scores.
source: As in experiment 1, individuals with low general factor scores showed greater adjustment of learning rate to volatility, learning faster in the volatile block than the stable block, than participants with high general factor scores.
evidence: Interpretation of the negative regression coefficient, with explicit comparison to experiment 1.

claim: In experiment 2, individuals with low scores on the general internalizing factor showed greater increases in learning rates in the volatile relative to stable task block following better-than-expected versus worse-than-expected outcomes.
source: As in experiment 1, individuals with low scores on the general internalizing factor showed greater increases in learning rates in the volatile relative to stable task block following better-than-expected versus worse-than-expected outcomes.
evidence: Interpretation of modeling results with explicit comparison to experiment 1.

claim: In experiment 2, the boost in learning from positive predictions errors under volatile conditions was absent in individuals with high general factor scores.
source: This boost in learning from positive predictions errors under volatile conditions was absent in individuals with high general factor scores; as in experiment 1, if anything, individuals with high general factor scores' learning after positive outcomes was reduced under volatile relative to stable conditions
evidence: Interpretation of modeling results illustrated in Figure 5b, with explicit comparison to experiment 1.

claim: A failure to boost learning when contingencies are volatile, especially following a better than expected outcome, is a shared characteristic of both anxiety and depression.
source: These findings, alongside those from experiment 1, indicate that a failure to boost learning when contingencies are volatile, especially following a better than expected outcome, is a shared characteristic of both anxiety and depression.
evidence: Inference drawn from the pattern of results across both experiments showing general factor but not specific factor effects.

claim: Across both experiments, high scores on the general factor were associated with reduced adjustment of learning rate to volatility.
source: Across both experiments, we observed that high scores on the general factor were associated with reduced adjustment of learning rate to volatility.
evidence: Summary statement of main finding across both experiments.

claim: No parallel relationship between learning rate adjustment to volatility and scores on the anxiety or depression-specific factors was observed.
source: No parallel relationship was observed for scores on the anxiety or depression-specific factors.
evidence: Summary statement of null findings for specific factors across both experiments.

claim: Impoverished adaptation of learning to contingency volatility is linked to the common component of anxiety and depressive symptomatology.
source: These findings are in line with the contention that impoverished adaptation of learning to contingency volatility is linked to the common component of anxiety and depressive symptomatology.
evidence: Inference drawn from the pattern of results showing general factor but not specific factor effects.

claim: Neither experiment found evidence to suggest that the relationship between impoverished adaptation of learning rate to volatility and scores on the general internalizing factor was modulated by outcome domain.
source: Neither experiment found any evidence to suggest that the relationship between impoverished adaptation of learning rate to volatility and scores on the general internalizing factor was modulated by outcome domain.
evidence: Summary statement of null findings for domain-specificity across both experiments.

claim: Across all three versions of the task, individuals with low general factor scores showed greater adaptation of learning rate to volatility than individuals with high general factor scores.
source: Across all three versions of the task, individuals with low general factor scores showed greater adaptation of learning rate to volatility than individuals with high general factor scores.
evidence: Summary statement of main finding across all task versions.

claim: The impairment in adjusting learning to volatility linked to elevated internalizing symptoms generalizes across both reward and punishment learning.
source: This suggests that the impairment in adjusting learning to volatility linked to elevated internalizing symptoms generalizes across both reward and punishment learning.
evidence: Inference drawn from the lack of domain-specific effects across experiments.

claim: It has previously been suggested that anxiety might be especially associated with altered learning regarding punishment.
source: It has previously been suggested that anxiety might be especially associated with altered learning regarding punishment (Lissek et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: It has been suggested that depression might be especially associated with altered learning regarding reward.
source: whereas depression might be especially associated with altered learning regarding reward (Elliott et al., 1997; Steele et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Recent reviews have suggested that evidence for depression being especially associated with altered reward learning is far from clear cut.
source: However, recent reviews have suggested that evidence for the latter, at least, is far from clear cut (Robinson and Chase, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to a recent review.

claim: Two previous studies found elevated trait anxiety to be linked to impoverished learning rate adjustment when outcomes involved punishment.
source: In the case of the volatility task used here, two previous studies found elevated trait anxiety to be linked to impoverished learning rate adjustment when outcomes involved punishment (electric stimulation or financial loss; Browning et al., 2015; Pulcu and Browning, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: For outcomes involving reward gain, the correlations between trait anxiety and learning rate adaptation to volatility in prior studies were not credibly different from zero but also not credibly different to that observed with punishing outcomes.
source: For outcomes involving reward gain, the correlations between trait anxiety and learning rate adaptation to volatility were not credibly different from zero but also not credibly different to that observed with punishing outcomes (Browning et al., 2015; Pulcu and Browning, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The STAI trait scale does not provide a particularly pure measure of anxiety-specific affect, also showing moderate-to-high correlations with measures of depression.
source: In addition, as touched on in the Introduction, the measure of anxiety used (the STAI trait scale) does not provide a particularly pure measure of anxiety-specific affect, also showing moderate-to-high correlations with measures of depression.
evidence: Statement about the psychometric properties of the STAI, drawing on established knowledge in the field.

claim: There was no evidence to support a relationship between anxiety-specific symptoms and enhanced learning following punishing versus rewarding outcomes.
source: Considering anxiety first, we found no evidence to support a relationship between anxiety-specific symptoms and enhanced learning following punishing versus rewarding outcomes
evidence: Summary statement of null findings for anxiety-specific effects.

claim: There was no evidence to support a differential relationship between anxiety-specific symptoms and adaptation of learning to volatility when outcomes are punishing versus rewarding.
source: or to suggest a differential relationship between anxiety-specific symptoms and adaptation of learning to volatility when outcomes are punishing versus rewarding.
evidence: Summary statement of null findings for anxiety-specific effects.

claim: There was no evidence to support a relationship between depression-specific symptoms and differential adaptation of learning to volatility as a function of outcome domain.
source: There was also no evidence to support a relationship between depression-specific symptoms and differential adaptation of learning to volatility as a function of outcome domain.
evidence: Summary statement of null findings for depression-specific effects.

claim: The deficit in adapting learning rate to volatility is linked to symptom variance common to anxiety and depression and is general to both learning about reward and learning about punishment.
source: These findings, together with those for the general factor reviewed above, suggest that the deficit in adapting learning rate to volatility is linked to symptom variance common to anxiety and depression and is general to both learning about reward and learning about punishment.
evidence: Inference drawn from the pattern of results across both experiments.

claim: Individuals with low scores on the general internalizing factor mainly showed a volatility-related boost to learning from positive prediction errors.
source: Here, across both experiments, we observed that individuals with low scores on the general internalizing factor mainly showed a volatility-related boost to learning from positive prediction errors.
evidence: Summary statement of findings across both experiments.

claim: The selective boost to learning from positive prediction errors when contingencies were volatile was not shown by individuals with high scores on the general internalizing factor.
source: This selective boost to learning from positive prediction errors when contingencies were volatile was not shown by individuals with high scores on the general internalizing factor.
evidence: Summary statement of findings across both experiments.

claim: Asymmetry in learning from positive versus negative prediction errors does not confer a performance advantage in the current task given that both outcome types are equally fully informative.
source: In the current task, asymmetry in learning from positive versus negative prediction errors does not confer a performance advantage given that both outcome types are equally fully informative—receiving a good outcome following selection of shape 1 means shape 2 would have resulted in a bad outcome and vice versa.
evidence: Logical inference about task structure and information content of outcomes.

claim: Asymmetric learning from good versus bad outcomes under volatility might be valuable in many real-world situations.
source: However, asymmetric learning from good versus bad outcomes under volatility might be valuable in many real-world situations.
evidence: Speculation about the potential adaptive value of the observed learning pattern.

claim: When the world changes, there might normally be fewer ways of performing well than performing badly, so learning more substantially from the former could be advantageous.
source: Conceivably, when the world changes, there might normally be fewer ways of performing well than performing badly, so learning more substantially from the former could be advantageous (Huys et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculation supported by citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: Enhanced learning from positive prediction errors when the world is volatile might reflect a learning style acquired over time by individuals with low general factor scores and applied by default in new situations.
source: As such, enhanced learning from positive prediction errors when the world is volatile might reflect a learning style acquired over time by individuals with low general factor scores and applied by default in new situations, such as the current tasks.
evidence: Speculation about the origin and nature of the observed learning pattern.

claim: The development of interventions aimed at assisting participants to better distinguish contingency noise from contingency volatility might be useful in treatment of both anxiety and depression.
source: Given the ubiquity of volatility in the real-world, our findings suggest that the development of interventions aimed at assisting participants to better distinguish contingency noise from contingency volatility, and to adjust decisions accordingly, might be useful in treatment of both anxiety and depression.
evidence: Speculation about potential clinical applications based on the findings.

claim: Impoverished adjustment of learning rate to volatility is broadly linked to internalizing psychopathology.
source: In summary, our findings provide support for the contention that impoverished adjustment of learning rate to volatility is broadly linked to internalizing psychopathology.
evidence: Summary inference drawn from the overall pattern of results.

claim: The deficit in adjusting learning to volatility is linked to symptoms shared by both anxious and depressed individuals, with no additional relationship being observed for anxiety or depression specific symptoms.
source: Bifactor modeling of internalizing symptoms and hierarchical Bayesian modeling of task performance enabled us to establish that this deficit is linked to symptoms shared by both anxious and depressed individuals, that is, to scores on a general internalizing factor, with no additional relationship being observed for anxiety or depression specific symptoms.
evidence: Summary inference drawn from the overall pattern of results.

claim: The relationship between general factor scores and impaired adaptation of learning to volatility was observed in a sample including participants with anxiety and depressive disorders as well as in an online sample where no diagnostic interviews or pre-screening on symptoms was conducted.
source: The relationship between general factor scores and impaired adaptation of learning to volatility was observed in a sample including participants with anxiety and depressive disorders as well as in an online sample where no diagnostic interviews or pre-screening on symptoms was conducted.
evidence: Summary statement about the generalizability of findings across samples.

claim: The relationship between general factor scores and impaired adaptation of learning to volatility held regardless of whether outcomes entailed receipt of reward, shock or reward loss.
source: Further, this relationship held regardless of whether outcomes entailed receipt of reward, shock or reward loss. This speaks to the generality of the deficit in question.
evidence: Summary statement about the generalizability of findings across outcome types.

claim: The ability to boost learning under volatility following better-than-expected outcomes could potentially confer resilience when faced with environments characterized by second-order uncertainty.
source: It is possible that in everyday life, a generally adaptive strategy when the world is rapidly changing is to learn from successful actions. The ability to do this could potentially confer resilience when faced with environments characterized by second-order uncertainty.
evidence: Speculation about the potential adaptive value of the observed learning pattern.

claim: For individuals with high levels of internalizing symptoms, the inability to adjust behavior depending on whether unexpected outcomes are likely due to contingency noise or to contingency volatility might well comprise decision-making across multiple settings.
source: In contrast, for individuals with high levels of internalizing symptoms, the inability to adjust behavior depending on whether unexpected outcomes are likely due to contingency noise or to contingency volatility might well comprise decision-making across multiple settings
evidence: Speculation about the broader implications of the observed deficit.

claim: The inability to adjust behavior to different sources of uncertainty could explain findings that self-reported intolerance of uncertainty is elevated in individuals with both anxiety and depressive disorders.
source: this could explain findings that self-reported intolerance of uncertainty is elevated in individuals with both anxiety and depressive disorders.
evidence: Speculation linking the current findings to prior observations in the literature.

claim: Greater specification of the manner in which deficits in decision-making map onto latent dimensions of psychopathology will play an important role in the advancement of personalized medicine.
source: More generally, we believe that greater specification of the manner in which deficits in decision-making, and other cognitive functions, map onto latent dimensions of psychopathology will play an important role in the advancement of personalized medicine
evidence: Speculation about the broader implications of this research approach.

claim: Healthy adult participants are able to adjust their rate of updating to match contingency volatility.
source: Behrens et al., 2007 reported that healthy adult participants are indeed able to adjust their rate of updating, that is, their learning rate, to match contingency volatility in this manner.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Trait anxiety was associated with reduced adaptation of learning rate to volatility in an aversive version of the probabilistic decision-making task.
source: Modeling participants' performance on an aversive version of Behrens and colleagues' probabilistic decision-making task, using electrical stimulation as outcomes, we found that trait anxiety was associated with reduced adaptation of learning rate to volatility.
evidence: Reference to findings from prior work by the authors.

claim: Scores on the Spielberger Trait Anxiety Inventory are typically elevated across patients with both anxiety and depressive disorders.
source: Scores on the Spielberger Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI, Spielberger et al., 1983), the measure of anxiety used in Browning et al., 2015, are typically elevated across patients with both anxiety and depressive disorders
evidence: Statement about the psychometric properties of the STAI, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: STAI scores correlate highly with scores on measures of depression such as the Beck Depression Inventory.
source: and correlate highly with scores on measures of depression such as the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI, Beck et al., 1961).
evidence: Statement about the psychometric properties of the STAI, drawing on established knowledge and citation.

claim: Intolerance of uncertainty has been proposed as a core feature of generalized anxiety disorder.
source: In recognition of this, intolerance of uncertainty has been proposed as a core feature of generalized anxiety disorder (Freeston et al., 1994; Dugas et al., 1998; Dugas et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Intolerance of uncertainty has been proposed as a transdiagnostic marker of internalizing psychopathology more broadly.
source: and, more recently, a transdiagnostic marker of internalizing psychopathology more broadly (Gentes and Ruscio, 2011; Carleton et al., 2012; Boswell et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The neural substrate and affective consequences of learning from unexpected outcomes may vary both with domain (reward versus punishment) and with whether outcomes are better or worse than expected.
source: There is evidence that the neural substrate, and affective consequences, of learning from unexpected outcomes may vary both with domain (reward versus punishment; Boureau and Dayan, 2011) and with whether outcomes are better or worse than expected (Frank et al., 2007; Cox et al., 2015; Eldar et al., 2016; Palminteri and Pessiglione, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature.
